title: Pune Lab's HPV Self-Sampling Kit Aims to Expand Cervical Cancer Screening
excerpt: Greenarray Labs has launched CerviSens, a vaginal self-sampling kit for high-risk HPV testing that skips the speculum exam. A 203-sample validation study reported 98.0% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity versus clinician collection.
body:
• Pune-based Greenarray Labs has launched CerviSens, a vaginal self-sampling kit that lets women collect their own sample for high-risk HPV testing — without a speculum examination at the time of collection.
  • In a 203-sample validation study published in Frontiers in Medical Technology in September 2025, self-collected samples matched clinician-collected ones at 98.0% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity for HPV detection.
  • What this means for you: If you have been putting off cervical screening because of discomfort, embarrassment, or privacy concerns, ask your doctor or an NABL-accredited lab about HPV self-sampling options. CerviSens is a licensed Class A medical device (Licence No. MFG/IVD/2020/000011), and the company says women who test positive are counselled and connected to follow-up care.
  • Cervical cancer kills nearly 79,000 Indian women a year — India accounts for 21% of the world's cases — yet only about 1.9% of Indian women are screened.

A Pune laboratory has launched a self-sampling kit for cervical cancer screening that allows women to collect their own vaginal sample for human papillomavirus testing — eliminating the pelvic examination with a speculum that keeps many women from getting screened at all.

Greenarray Labs' CerviSens kit is designed to attack the access barriers that have kept India's cervical screening rates near the floor: the need to visit a healthcare facility, a trained healthcare professional, and an intimate examination that many women find awkward or embarrassing. The collected sample is tested in a laboratory for high-risk HPV, which is associated with the majority of cervical cancer cases.

The approach has been clinically validated. A study published in Frontiers in Medical Technology in September 2025 evaluated 203 paired self-collected and clinician-collected samples and reported 98.0% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity for HPV detection, using clinician-collected samples as the reference standard.

Context & Background

Cervical cancer is one of the few cancers where screening genuinely saves lives — it is largely preventable through HPV vaccination, regular screening and timely treatment. Yet India contributes 21% of the world's cervical cancer cases, accounting for nearly 79,000 deaths among Indian women each year — roughly two-thirds of diagnosed cases, a sign of late-stage detection. As few as 1.9% of Indian women are screened, according to a 2020 national survey.

https://x.com/SerumInstIndia/status/2107019056369057902

The World Health Organization endorses HPV DNA testing as the first-choice screening method for cervical cancer prevention, and its elimination strategy rests on three pillars: vaccination, screening and timely treatment. Self-sampling is not new globally, but validated Indian-made kits are rare — Metropolis Healthcare's partnership with Roche Diagnostics on a self-sampling HPV DNA test is the other notable domestic entry.

Beyond the kit, Greenarray has been mapping HPV genotypes across India. A five-year multicentric study of 12,373 samples from Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha and Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh found 2.6% positivity for high-risk HPV, with about 63% of positive cases among women aged 31–50. HPV16 was the most frequently detected genotype, followed by HPV31, HPV33 and HPV18, and 34.5% of HPV-positive samples carried two or more high-risk genotypes. The test identifies 14 high-risk genotypes individually.

Impact & Analysis

The significance is in the funnel. Embarrassment, privacy concerns and distance from clinics are the documented drop-off points in India's screening pipeline, and a private self-collection step targets them directly. Dr. Sanjay Gupte, founder of Greenarray Labs, stressed that screening only works if positives reach treatment: "The important next step is ensuring that women who test positive are appropriately counselled and connected to further clinical evaluation and care."

"For screening to reach more women, it has to become easier to access and simpler to participate in. Our focus is on combining easier sample collection with validated laboratory testing and ensuring that screening ultimately leads to appropriate medical follow-up wherever required."

— Nitin Gupte, CEO, Greenarray Labs

Dr. Preeti Helkar, the company's chief genomic scientist, said individual genotyping — rather than lumping all non-16/18 types together — gives a more detailed picture of HPV patterns across populations and supports surveillance and clinical follow-up. The device is manufactured under India's Medical Devices Rules, 2017, and testing runs in an NABL-accredited laboratory with quality controls.

Diaspora Angle

For NRI families, the news lands close to home. Many overseas Indians arrange annual health checkups for relatives in India, and a self-sampling option is worth flagging to women back home who have skipped cervical screening. India's screening gap is also a known concern in diaspora health philanthropy, and validated low-cost Indian kits are the kind of intervention that scales through screening camps and NGO programmes.

What's Next

Pricing and distribution were not disclosed — watch whether hospitals and screening camps adopt the kit, and whether it enters state or national screening programmes. The broader test will be the one Dr. Gupte named: converting positive results into counselling, evaluation and treatment, the step where screening programmes most often fail.
